Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: At fifty-four, Ingrid had spent thirty years commanding her kitchen with quiet authority, but that authority had been shattered nine months ago when a male sous-chef she had personally mentored assaulted her in the walk‑in cooler. She could not find the words to describe what happened—the memory arrived as jagged fragments: the click of the latch, the cold steel shelving pressing into her back, the crushing weight of his body pinning her in the same position she now finds herself in whenever the memory surfaces. That visceral bodily reenactment was the only language her memory spoke, and it left her wordless, unable to narrate the event even to herself. What she could articulate was the betrayal. She had trusted him, trained him; his attack had rewired her understanding of the world: people cannot be trusted, you never know who will harm you. Now, certain conversations—a coworker’s offhand comment about loyalty, an earnest compliment from a regular customer—made her stomach turn. When a male server lingered too long at her station, her throat tightened. Emotional closeness, whether from a concerned friend or a warm exchange with a line cook, felt like a setup for another betrayal. Each time someone stepped too close or a conversation veered toward intimacy, the fragmented images of the cooler flooded back—the metal, the weight—and each time, the memory hardened her belief that she was foolish to have trusted anyone. Because she now lived with the conviction that harm could come from anyone, Ingrid had become hypervigilant. She startled at the sudden movement of a waiter’s hand reaching for a plate. Strangers approaching the kitchen entrance made her breath catch as though they were coming for her. These startle responses themselves triggered the fragmented memories, and each wave of fear confirmed that her distrust was justified—the world was indeed dangerous. Her mistrust had also reshaped what she noticed: she now scanned conversations for hidden menace, which meant that even ordinary topics like a coworker’s marriage troubles became triggers for her. Her constant alertness meant that she was acutely aware of every man who entered her vicinity, making male presence a near-constant trigger. The recurring intrusive memory, with its wordless reenactment, was a relentless reminder of her vulnerability, deepening her sense of betrayal with each recurrence. The conviction that she should have seen it coming kept pulling her back into the memory, as if her own failure had locked the door behind her. She had begun delegating the closing duties to her female sous‑chef, never staying late alone. Her husband, Tomas, noticed she had stopped inviting friends over, and their own conversations had grown stilted as she avoided any topic that felt too personal. What brought her to the clinic was a panic attack during a dinner service when a male customer reached across the counter to thank her. She had frozen, her body locked into that same position, and had to be led from the kitchen. She is afraid that she will never be able to work again, but more than that, she is terrified of the person she has become—someone who sees a threat in every friendly gesture.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., distrust, betrayal) directly cause or trigger the intrusive memory. The memory is triggered by external cues or startle responses, not by the beliefs themselves.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
